newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia to meet telecom deregulation challenges.
newsitem.headline: Asia to meet telecom deregulation challenges.

text.p: Asian countries will draw the bulk of technology business in the next century but governments and business must prepare to cope with challenges to culture and sovereignty, industry experts said on Thursday.
Investments were flowing to the region but profitability could be slowed by social and political policies, they said.
The industry officials were speaking at a forum during the Asia Telecom '97 trade fair.

"The major problem is deregulation. OECD (Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development) countries worry about the loss of jobs," Bobby Choonavala, president for Asia Pacific operations at Digital Equipment Corp said.
He said there were fears of losing control and revenue to global companies but Internet and deregulation would continue to accelerate information development in these countries.
Hong Chen, chairman and president of AimQuest Corp agreed that the deployment of modern infrastructure ought to make the ground fertile for strategic international alliances.
"In Asian countries there are lots of regulation issues. These are based on pride, like being the only telecommunications company," Chen said.
He predicted that Internet would provide for collective cross-border information systems, such as was already possible with roaming phone services like Global Systems Mobile (GSM).
Some experts said Asia's information providers would also have to consider how much to spend on social responsibility.
"This region is concerned with decency and morality issues," said Attila Elci, senior expert of the Pakistan Telecom Company.

He said this was an age of open communication channels with no such thing as local content once it was placed on Internet. He suggested content could be tagged with classification codes, as in television, to alert users.
To avoid cultural hegemony, Michael Reede of Australia's Gilbert & Tobin said countries in Asia should promote an environment for the building of local content sites.
"Rather than blocking out content in the net heavy U.S. market website, try and build content here."
Some countries, however, will advertantly set aside traditional considerations.
Singapore, Malaysia and Hong Kong, for example, were more aggressive in pushing cultural frontiers.
This was partly because of the necessity for information in their competitive business environments, one panelist said.
